family.olivetti-m.description: Olivetti’s M-designated desktops, transportables and laptops: different architectures grouped by commercial name.
family.olivetti-m.history:
The M designation spans several stages of Olivetti personal computing. This catalogue groups professional desktops, transportables and laptops under it, but not a single architecture: a shared letter does not imply a shared motherboard, firmware or peripherals. Model numbers alone do not establish a direct succession.

Introduced in 1982, the M20 used a Zilog Z8001 and its own PCOS environment. The M24, presented at Hannover in March 1984, took a different direction: IBM PC compatibility, an Intel 8086 and access to MS-DOS software. Distribution as the AT&T PC 6300 illustrates how an Olivetti platform could reach another market under another name without becoming an AT&T design.

Portable computing developed alongside desktops. The 1983 M10 offered a small tool with an LCD; the 1984 M21 combined a built-in monitor with a keyboard that closed over it, a transportable solution. The 1987 M15 and 1988 M15 Plus belong to another stage: PC compatibility and LCDs, reflective on M15 and backlit on Plus. Their configurations and upgrades are not interchangeable.

The M28, M250 and M280 illustrate the expansion of 286 compatibles, while the M380 and M300 variants represent later PC generations. Suffixes and revisions matter: a general model name can cover different boards and processors. The table distinguishes historical milestones from models researched by BluMach. It is an expandable selection, not the complete Olivetti catalogue. In this alpha, M15 and M15 Plus sheets offer experimental creation; mentioning other models here neither enables nor certifies their emulation.
